lessons.title: Inspecting and Cleaning the Frame
lessons.body: Start by placing the frame on a clean, flat surface like a wooden pallet or a sturdy table. You need good lightâwork outdoors or use a bright LED lamp. Put on safety glasses and gloves. First, check for any bends, cracks, or deep rust. Look closely at the steering head tube, the swingarm pivot area, and the rear shock mounts. A cracked frame is dangerous; if you find one, set it aside and get a replacement. For minor rust, use a wire brush or sandpaper (80-grit then 120-grit) to remove it. In humid coastal areas like Mombasa or Lagos, rust spreads fast, so treat any bare metal immediately with a rust converter like phosphoric acid. Next, clean the frame with a degreaser. Mix dish soap with warm water if you don't have a dedicated degreaser. Use a stiff nylon brush to scrub away dirt, oil, and grease. Pay attention to welds and tight corners where grime hides. Rinse with clean water and dry with a cloth. Then wipe down with acetone or methylated spirits to remove any residue. This step is critical because paint and threadlocker won't stick to oily surfaces. After cleaning, inspect all threaded holes. Run a tap (M6, M8, M10) through them to clear paint or rust. If a thread is stripped, you can install a Helicoil insert. Finally, check the frame's alignment by placing a straight edge along the main tube. Any gap greater than 2 mm means the frame is bent. For African workshops, a simple plumb bob and string can check vertical alignment. Once clean and straight, apply a thin coat of primer if you plan to paint, or leave bare for assembly. Always store the frame on a padded surface to avoid scratches.

lessons.title: Mounting the Frame on Assembly Jig
lessons.body: An assembly jig holds the frame steady while you install heavy components. You can build a simple jig using square steel tubes (40x40 mm) welded to a base plate. The jig must be level; use a spirit level to check both directions. If you don't have a welder, bolt together wooden beams (100x100 mm) with M12 bolts. Place the frame onto the jig so the steering head and swingarm pivot are supported. The frame should not rock. Use C-clamps or U-bolts to secure it. For a typical EV motorbike frame, the steering head tube should be about 800-900 mm from the ground, and the swingarm pivot about 300-350 mm. Measure these heights with a tape measure. If your jig is adjustable, set these dimensions. Next, check that the frame is horizontal side-to-side. Place a spirit level across the top tubes. If it's off, shim the low side with metal plates. Once level, tighten all clamps. Now you can test fit the swingarm and rear shock. The jig should allow you to remove and install parts without the frame moving. In many African workshops, a jig made from scrap metal and a wooden pallet works fine. Just ensure it's stable. After mounting, mark the jig with a paint pen for future frames. This saves time on the next build. Remember, a wobbly frame leads to misaligned wheels and poor handling. Take 10 minutes to get it right.

lessons.title: Installing Steering Head Bearings
lessons.body: The steering head bearings let the front fork turn smoothly. Most EV motorbikes use tapered roller bearings. You need a bearing driver, a hammer, and grease. First, clean the steering head tube inside. Use a rag with solvent. Then apply a thin layer of high-temperature grease to the inside of the tube. Take the lower bearing cone (the inner race) and press it onto the steering stem using a pipe or bearing driver. Tap evenly until it seats fully. You'll hear a change in sound. Next, pack the bearing with grease. Work grease into the rollers by hand. For the upper bearing, place it into the top of the head tube. Then insert the steering stem through the head tube. Install the upper cone and dust seal. Thread on the adjusting nut. Tighten it by hand until snug, then use a spanner to turn it another 1/8 to 1/4 turn. You want zero play but no binding. Check by turning the fork side to side; it should move smoothly with slight resistance. If it feels gritty, the bearings are not seated or are damaged. In dusty African conditions, use sealed bearings if available. Otherwise, pack extra grease. After adjustment, install the lock nut and tighten it while holding the adjusting nut. Torque the lock nut to 25-30 Nm. Recheck play after tightening. A common mistake is overtightening, which causes flat spots and dangerous handling. Test ride at low speed to confirm.

lessons.title: Attaching Swingarm and Rear Suspension
lessons.body: The swingarm connects the rear wheel to the frame. Start by greasing the swingarm pivot bolt and the bearings inside the swingarm. Use a waterproof grease like lithium complex. Slide the swingarm into the frame's pivot brackets. Insert the pivot bolt from the left side. Apply threadlocker (blue Loctite) to the bolt threads. Thread on the nut and tighten to 60-70 Nm for a typical M14 bolt. Do not overtighten; you'll crush the bearings. Check that the swingarm moves up and down freely without side play. If it's tight, the bearings are misaligned. Next, install the rear shock absorbers. Most EV bikes have twin shocks. Mount the top eye to the frame and the bottom eye to the swingarm. Use new mounting bolts and nuts. Torque the shock bolts to 40-45 Nm. For the shock preload, set it to the middle position for a rider of 70-80 kg. In Africa, roads can be rough, so you might increase preload by 2 clicks. Check that the shock springs don't rub on the swingarm or frame. Finally, install the rear wheel temporarily to check alignment. The wheel should be centered between the swingarm legs. Use a string line from the front wheel to the rear wheel to check tracking. Adjust the chain adjusters if needed. After everything is tight, bounce the rear suspension a few times. Listen for clunks. If you hear any, something is loose. Recheck all bolts.

lessons.title: Front Fork Installation and Alignment
lessons.body: Front forks hold the wheel and absorb bumps. Begin by sliding the fork tubes into the triple clamps. The lower triple clamp holds the tubes; the upper clamp secures them. Leave the upper clamp bolts loose for now. Push the tubes up until they protrude about 10-15 mm above the upper clamp. This height affects steering. For most EV motorbikes, 10 mm is a good starting point. Tighten the lower clamp bolts to 20-25 Nm. Then tighten the upper clamp bolts to 20-25 Nm. Do not overtighten; you can crack the aluminum clamp. Next, install the front wheel. Slide the axle through the fork dropouts and wheel hub. Tighten the axle nut to 50-60 Nm. Check that the wheel spins freely. Now check alignment. Stand in front of the bike and look at the fork tubes. They should be parallel. If one tube is forward or backward, loosen the clamps and adjust. Use a straight edge against the fork tubes to check. Also, ensure the handlebar is straight. With the wheel pointing forward, the handlebar should be perpendicular to the frame. Adjust the handlebar clamps if needed. Finally, check the fork oil. Most forks need 150-200 ml of 10W fork oil per leg. If you don't know the history, drain and refill. In dusty conditions, change fork oil every 5000 km. After installation, compress the forks a few times to settle the springs. Then recheck all bolts.

lessons.title: Torque Specifications for Chassis Fasteners
lessons.body: Torque is the tightness of a bolt, measured in Newton-meters (Nm). Too loose, parts fall off. Too tight, bolts break or threads strip. You need a torque wrench. The click-type is best for beginners. Always use the correct size socket. For chassis fasteners on an EV motorbike, here are common specs: Steering stem lock nut: 25-30 Nm. Triple clamp bolts (M8): 20-25 Nm. Swingarm pivot bolt (M14): 60-70 Nm. Rear shock bolts (M10): 40-45 Nm. Front axle nut (M12): 50-60 Nm. Rear axle nut (M14): 80-90 Nm. Motor mount bolts (M10): 45-50 Nm. Battery box bolts (M8): 15-20 Nm. Always clean threads and apply threadlocker (blue) unless specified dry. Tighten in a crisscross pattern for multiple bolts, like on a wheel. After torquing, mark the bolt and nut with a paint pen so you can see if it loosens. Recheck torque after the first 50 km and then every 1000 km. In African heat, metal expands, so torque can change. Keep a torque chart in your workshop. If you don't have a torque wrench, tighten until snug plus a quarter turn for small bolts, but this is risky. Save up for a good wrench; it's cheaper than replacing a stripped frame. Always use a calibrated wrench. Store it at its lowest setting.

quiz.q: What should you use to remove minor rust from a frame?
quiz.explanation: Wire brush or sandpaper abrades rust away without damaging the frame.

quiz.q: Why is it important to clean the frame with acetone before painting?
options: B) To remove oil and residue
quiz.explanation: Acetone removes oils and residues so paint and threadlocker can adhere properly.

quiz.q: What is the maximum acceptable gap when checking frame alignment with a straight edge?
quiz.explanation: A gap greater than 2 mm indicates the frame is bent and unsafe.

quiz.q: What tool can be used to check vertical alignment of a frame?
quiz.explanation: A plumb bob and string provide a simple vertical reference for alignment.

quiz.q: What should you apply to bare metal after cleaning to prevent rust?
quiz.explanation: Rust converter like phosphoric acid treats bare metal and prevents new rust.

quiz.q: What is the recommended height for the steering head tube on a jig?
quiz.explanation: Steering head tube should be about 800-900 mm from the ground for typical EV motorbike frames.

quiz.q: What material can be used to build a simple assembly jig?
quiz.explanation: Square steel tubes welded to a base plate provide a sturdy jig.

quiz.q: Why should the frame be level on the jig?
options: B) To prevent misalignment of wheels
quiz.explanation: A level frame ensures proper alignment of wheels and handling.

quiz.q: What is used to secure the frame to the jig?
quiz.explanation: C-clamps or U-bolts hold the frame securely without movement.

quiz.q: What is the recommended height for the swingarm pivot on a jig?
quiz.explanation: Swingarm pivot should be about 300-350 mm from the ground.

quiz.q: What type of bearings are commonly used in the steering head?
quiz.explanation: Tapered roller bearings handle both radial and axial loads in steering heads.

quiz.q: How should you pack a steering head bearing with grease?
options: B) Work grease in by hand
quiz.explanation: Working grease into the rollers by hand ensures full coverage.

quiz.q: What is the correct torque for the steering stem lock nut?
quiz.explanation: Lock nut torque is typically 25-30 Nm to secure adjustment without overloading.

quiz.q: What should you check after tightening the steering head bearings?
quiz.explanation: Check for zero play and smooth turning to ensure proper bearing adjustment.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when adjusting steering head bearings?
quiz.explanation: Over-tightening causes flat spots and dangerous handling.

quiz.q: What should you apply to the swingarm pivot bolt threads before installation?
quiz.explanation: Threadlocker (blue Loctite) prevents the bolt from loosening due to vibration.

quiz.q: What is the typical torque for the swingarm pivot bolt (M14)?
quiz.explanation: M14 swingarm pivot bolts typically require 60-70 Nm.

quiz.q: How can you check rear wheel alignment?
quiz.explanation: A string line from front to rear wheel checks tracking and alignment.

quiz.q: What should you do after installing the rear suspension?
quiz.explanation: Bouncing helps settle components and reveal any loose parts or clunks.

quiz.q: What is the recommended torque for rear shock bolts (M10)?
quiz.explanation: M10 shock bolts typically require 40-45 Nm.

quiz.q: How much should the fork tubes protrude above the upper triple clamp?
quiz.explanation: 10-15 mm protrusion is a common starting point for handling.

quiz.q: What is the torque for the front axle nut (M12)?
quiz.explanation: Front axle nut (M12) typically requires 50-60 Nm.

quiz.q: What should you use to check fork tube parallelism?
quiz.explanation: A straight edge against the fork tubes shows if they are parallel.

quiz.q: How often should fork oil be changed in dusty conditions?
quiz.explanation: Dusty conditions contaminate fork oil, so change every 5000 km.

quiz.q: What type of torque wrench is best for beginners?
quiz.explanation: Click-type torque wrenches are easy to use and reliable for beginners.

quiz.q: What is the torque specification for the rear axle nut (M14)?
quiz.explanation: Rear axle nut (M14) typically requires 80-90 Nm.

quiz.q: Why should you mark torqued bolts with a paint pen?
options: B) To see if they loosen
quiz.explanation: Paint marks provide a quick visual check for loosening.

quiz.q: What is the torque for motor mount bolts (M10)?
quiz.explanation: Motor mount bolts (M10) typically require 45-50 Nm.

quiz.q: How often should you recheck chassis fastener torque?
quiz.explanation: Recheck torque after first 50 km and then every 1000 km to ensure safety.

quiz.q: What should you do if you don't have a torque wrench?
options: A) Tighten as hard as possible
B) Use a quarter turn after snug
quiz.explanation: A quarter turn after snug is a risky but common field method for small bolts.
